review:
So, Kathy Rain. I don't usually write reviews, so this could be a little janky, but bear with me 'cause I think this is worthwhile to say.

--Characters and World

This game shines in characterbuilding. Not a single person (except one who is meant to be) feels out of place or annoying to encounter, and Kathy as a character both suits the position she's found herself in and has a personality you immediately recognize (Jerk with a Heart of Gold). She makes for an excellent protagonist, equally intelligent and witty with a personality that not only shows through her dialogue, but also through the solutions to some of the more impromptu puzzles you face. Rarely does she overstep believable bounds, and even the clues she gives you about objects you find do not come off as patronizing.

In other words, the voice acting and writing is spot-on, just as it needs to be for a story-driven point'n'click puzzler.

Not much needs to be said about the world, as it is for all intents and purposes semi-rural America, before cellphones were invented. Nothing noteworthy is changed, a few things are added (related to the plot), but otherwise it is entirely vanilla and well-represented. 

--Puzzles and Difficulty

Difficulty curve is notoriously hard to judge when it comes to puzzles, and often one individual will find some easier than others regardless of the intent. Despite that, Kathy Rain seems to have taken that a step further with puzzles that are far easier than the one that came before it found late in the game, and the hardest puzzles taking place in the second few hours. Thankfully, Kathy herself will at least let you know if you are on the right track with the harder puzzles, and stays silent when her suggestions aren't solicited. Most solutions (all but one, if I recall correctly) use a 'the easiest answer is the correct answer' policy, and (again, all but one) operate within the bounds of logic- even when reaching an area of the game where logic seems to have no meaning.

Puzzles can invariably be solved just by using the mouse- there is no keyboard usage save for where it makes obvious sense to do so (such as when typing), and even that is extremely rare. If you can't click it, you don't need to worry about it. There is no 'hunt the pixel' gameplay, either- all the items you interact with are well-lampshaded and easy to see, to the point where some of them might as well be draped in neon lights.

Overall, I found Kathy Rain very easy to get through, only having to consult a walkthrough once when I was missing a crucial item. Long-standing lovers of point and clicks will find this a walk in the park, whereas newcomers (are there any?) will find it a wading pool for the harder stuff. Most of these puzzles are character-driven as well, stemming from dialogue choices and showing the personalities and natures of those around Kathy (as well as Kathy herself), making them an integral part of the game rather than 'solve the soup can'-style pointlessness.

---Story and Pacing (no spoilers)

This is the one point where Kathy Rain falls a little short, and it isn't for lack of trying. The story begins excellently and at a medium burn, with the catalyst to adventure occuring soon after you start and with little backstory off the bat. Most of the backstory, in fact, is discovered over the course of the game with notes, dialogue and recorded messages, all of which (save one) is inevitably used in one way or another.

This persists throughout the game's middle in a way that never reaches a white-knuckle grip, but rather a leisurely jog with occasional rests that involve quick humor and fun characters (Goober, I'm looking at you). While there are the occasional twists, they never feel particularly jarring because of the slow speed with which you reach them, lessening their impact and dulling the edge- an edge that I think Kathy Rain sorely needed. Despite that, said twists and developments do grant a desire to keep playing, to remedy the events that go wrong and to wrap up the story. Players are pushed on, also, through small snippets of Kathy's past that she isn't particularly open about, but these have less of an effect both because of the ending and the way they are delivered.

As for the ending, this is where Kathy Rain loses much of its characters and world, instead making it solely about Kathy as a person- and unfortunately proving that she cannot stand on her own as an interesting protagonist. Kathy is at her best when interacting with others, but this last stretch involved only her and her own feelings amidst puzzles that are mostly 'placed' rather than 'organic', and without any of the witty dialogue or charm you find in earlier parts of the game (with a couple notable exceptions). The ending comes and goes, and it left me with a 'well, that happened' feeling that can only be described as mediocre- a sad thing for a game that had me interested and invested up until that point. Despite that, I can say that the more personal details of Kathy's choices earlier in life are handled well and intelligently (at least, on my playthrough. A different dialogue choice may yield a different result), without insulting individuals who have chosen to do the same in her place.

---End result

For a game with a new protagonist never seen before? Not half bad. Not half bad at all. For a point and clicker? Pretty frickin' decent. Is it worth fifteen bucks? That's harder to say. It is a short game, and depending on how quickly you burn through the puzzles at hand you may feel like you did not get your money's worth- especially considering the easy difficulty at hand. So since the puzzles are largely simple, lets judge it on characters and story alone. Would I hand Kathy and E fifteen bucks again, to help fund another investigation?

Fuck yeah, I would.

[b]“Whatever is rejected from the self, appears in the world as an event.” - C.G. Jung[/b]

As Clifftop Games' first project, [i]Kathy Rains[/i] is an intriguing work, which carries much promise for a future series, with invaluable psychoanalytical depth. When I picked this game, two things shined out as brilliant references: the 90s atmosphere displayed with the same engine used in [i]Blackwell[/i] series - another masterpiece of the adventure genre - and Dave Gilbert's name on voice direction department for the game, the creator of Rosa Blackwell himself. So it would be fair to assume Kathy would be an unexpected successor for Rosa. After I've completed the game, I sensed a completely different direction, yet I am much pleased with the outcome anyhow. Where [i]Blackwell[/i] was paranormal, [i]Kathy Rain[/i] could be described as psychoanalytical. Here, paranormal is a cosmetic layer rather than being context specific.

Kathy is a rebellious, snarky biker girl and an aspiring journalist major with a truckload of traumas, mainly concerning her family. Her good girl dorm mate Eileen brings into her attention that a certain "Joseph Rain" just passed away and whether he may be related to Kathy or not. He sure was - no other than Kathy's grandfather to be precise. Taking the news, Kathy takes off to attend the funeral, which opens a gate to her troubled past at the same time. As she investigates the recent demise and prior ailment of her grandfather which left him confided to a wheelchair, Kathy comes in contact with an uncanny mystery engulfing each and every corner of the silent, sleepy town of Conwell.

The storyline begins as an interesting enough detective mystery, yet quickly deviates from that context to take a seemingly supernatural path. Yet, under the layer of the supernatural, the game is - in my humble opinion - is a brilliant example for a psychoanalytical concept: the self and the shadow. According to Jungian psychology, every person bears an archetypal unconscious aspect that would be instinctual, illogical and wrapped in darkness; a mirroring opposite to our light, our self and the consciousness. This part is completely speculative on my behalf, and may contain spoilers, so feel free to skip to the next paragraph. [spoiler]Kathy's journey and her experiences throughout the game, are majorly symbolic acts of self-confrontation. The fictional red scythe flowers serve as hallucinogens which may be used for many psychedelic experiences of transcendence or self-discovery journeys - which explains most of Kathy's "supernatural" experiences. Thus, her main antagonist is herself all along, and all other figures are the ones that try to take similar journeys like her, yet failing to make peace with their own shadows. The antagonistic "Crimson One" is the personification for the hallucinogen flower itself. We already know that both Kathy's parents were somewhat into the consumption of the same drug also. Other characters involved, and their experiences may be explained in a similar manner. Yet, these are all my own speculations and interpretations. In the end, Kathy faces all her demons - her father's departure, her mother's insanity and her guilt driven from committing her into an asylum, the abortion, even not being able to be a part of her grandfather's life - and prevails. Thus, she leaves the hole and destroys the source of these symbolic drugs, preventing anyone who wouldn't be willful enough to face their own demons coming into harm.[/spoiler]

Kathy surely is not the most interesting of protagonists as we start, but as the game progresses, the storyline delivers. There are layers under her seemingly embittered and sarcastic personality, which makes her a realistic, even relatable character. Her relationship with Eileen is especially admirable, since she tries to protect her as if she is trying to protect her own extracted innocence. I regret that other characters were not as fleshed out as I would like, but they all serve their purpose within the plot.

We are familiar with the AGS engine already, and it is spectacular to see that the pixelated texture can present such admirable environment artwork and character designs. The game world itself was somewhat limited and the game time was short here, yet it is a great demonstration for the capabilities of the developer team. Voice acting, is really wondrous, with sincere emotions and character appropriate toning too, but since Dave Gilbert himself was responsible of that department, no less could be expected.

The gameplay? Well, it does not contain the most brilliant of puzzles, and sure has its logical impossibilities - like a scanner capable of copying sound files from cassette tapes, during 90s nonetheless - but I'd say it is quite alright as a whole. If you listen to the narrative itself and remarks made by characters all around, I'd say that you wouldn't have a hard time overall. It would probably take no longer than 5 hours or so to go through a complete playthrough, 6 if you'd go back for the achievements you've missed.

At the end of the day, sure, I'd recommend Kathy Rain but I'd also advise to take a %50 discount. The game is lovely, but it doesn't contain any replay value and quite short of an experience for the full price. I sincerely hope that we'd see a new adventure from Kathy in the future, which may explain various plot details that never see the light of day in this one. Enjoy!

This game's story is dumb, you guys.

Really dumb.

Look, I grew up on 90s point and click adventure games just like you ([i]in all likelihood, given that you're looking at this game.[/i]) And if you're looking for something that just captures the spirit of the era - look no further! It checks all the boxes, from the font choice to the art style. You'd swear up and down it was made in the same Scumm engine as Full Throttle and Day of The Tentacle. Hell, it even has the same issues with questionable voice acting quality - Kathy herself is generally well played, but the NPCs around her range from serviceable to downright atrocious.

But here's the thing - the story in this game... its [i]bad.[/i] It starts out fine - a young journalist comes back home to attend her grandfather's funeral, then gets caught up in the mystery of his sudden illness. Cool! But... about halfway through... something terrible happens.

The writers give up.

See, they set up a lot of loose threads to handle. And, frankly, loose threads are fun - they make for interesting stories. Forcing characters to deal with the implications of their decisions is at the heart of any good narrative. Buuuut... rather than commit to that, they start hand-waving in a VERY big way. Investigation starts giving way to "it's magic, yo". And, ultimately, every single major plotline is resolved through magical means. And not interesting, well fleshed out magic, either (looking your way, The Longest Journey.) No... just boring, half-thought-out dream visions and spirit quests.

It's deus ex machina on steroids. And what’s worse is it undercuts the core premise: its not Kathy’s investigation skills that solve the day, but instead these mystical forces directly spelling it out for her.

Look, you’re not a ~bad person~ if you like this game. Playing Kathy Rain won’t give you cancer or kill your dog or whatever.

But frankly, other than the obvious nostalgia hooks, this game is actually a lot weaker than many of the 90s games it mimics. The UX is bad. The game is short. The puzzles are generally so brainless that they’ll take you literally seconds to figure out. So all that leaves is the story it tells.

And guys? The story is [i][u]dumb.[/u]

I loved 90s point and click adventure games growing up, so I gave this a try. The atmosphere and art is nice, but three things turned me off. (1) The 90s nostalgia feels incomplete. Cathy doesn't look or sound like someone from the 90s (at least to me, who grew up in the 90s). She feels like a contemporary insert. (2) There was nothing that made me interested in playing as Cathy specifically and hearing her view point for the whole game, and that's largely because (3) She's a mean, unempathetic character. The example that really turned me off: Her grandmother, who just buried a loved one, invites her to chat and asks Kathy to tell her about her life. Kathy says, "Well, I ride a motorcycle, in case you missed it outside..." with this sarcastic lilt of "...you know, if you're an idiot." That's such an unnecessarily mean thing to say to your grieving grandmother who just invited you into her home after years of not talking, no hesitation or questions asked. Kathy talks like a un-socialized 15 yr old instead of a 20 year old journalism major.  Her wise-cracking sarcasm doesn't feel on point or badass, or even charmingly misguided. It feels abusive and solipsistic. 

If her sarcasm doesn't bother you, you might like this game. But as someone who's been on the receiving end of this "I'm lashing out with condescending snark to cover up my own hurt" bullying a good deal when I was a teenager (in the 90s), it really turns me off to the character. I think I'd rather play a game as her earnest roommate, who despite her seeming un-coolness, makes for an actually pretty badass detective with her organized notes and color printer.

Ugh Kathy Rain.  A game that is supposed to be following in the footsteps of Laura Bow, at least I’m pretty sure I read that somewhere.  Like Laura Bow you start out in College as a journalism major, unlike Laura Bow you seem to be a punk biker who is a sociopath.  At the end of the day though I quite liked the character of Kathy Rain and the other major character Eileen.  Their voice acting, what little there is, is good.  Whoever voices Kathy does a good job and the same goes for Eileen.  Since you do hear their voices the most, it’s pretty important for them to be pleasing.  That was one of the big problems with games like Gabriel Knight, Knight’s voice drove me nuts.  It was just awful.  The same goes for Laura Bow.  However, I can’t recommend this game too much is simply bad in it.  

Like that’s probably all the good stuff.  If a lot of stuff was good, I’d recommend the game, but most of it is quite bad.  So lets go with puzzles.  The game basically has very very very easy puzzles.  Which I guess would be fine, except I think they are also bad.  One puzzle required me to pick up a thermometer, which I attempted already pick up earlier in the game and couldn’t.  No dialogue or really anything lead me to think that later in the game I could now pick it up.  It’s the one puzzle I had to look online for a solution to.  Adventure games need to stop this, either let me pick up every single item I need when I see it, or I guess maybe MAYBE if you heavily stress the fact by the character saying something like, “oh I really need to get a thermometer, I think I saw one earlier I need to go back and get it.”  Then that MIGHT be acceptable.  Otherwise, never do this ever!  Almost every puzzle in this game can be solved in the area you are in, normally I would say this is fine, the problem here is that the areas are so small that it takes seconds to figure out puzzles.  That being said I guess I should give props to the game for having all the puzzles basically be logic puzzles as opposed to random math puzzles like a lot of adventure games do and which I hate.

Before getting into the story, I have to just add that one major problem with the game is the length.  It’s a big problem.  There are so few areas to explore.  Each area, might only have one or two screens to it.  You don’t really feel like you are exploring at all, which imo is critical in an adventure game.  The game also simply ends way too fast.  I suppose it’s possible to tell a short story, this game however fails at it.  There wasn’t any real time to get to know characters or have any feel for the town or even really to ponder what is going on in the game.  I’d say it feels more like watching a movie then playing a game, which I know a lot of games do these days, but I don’t like that.

However, the biggest problem is the story and I’m just going to count everything after this as spoilers.  [spoiler] The simple fact is this story makes no sense at all.  First of all I feel like it was a bait and switch.  I bought the game thinking it was going to be an epic murder mystery like a Laura Bow game.  Instead, I guess it’s a horror game? That’s really not the right word for it, it is a mystery, it’s just that the mystery is so terrible I can’t even really call it that.  I would say it’s a very poor version of an HP Lovecraft story.  Yup, that sounds about right.  

So for starters characters act in ways no one ever would.  Kathy is a sophomore in college majoring in journalism.  Her roommate Eileen is super Christian and I guess loves reading obituaries, because the game starts with her finding out that Kathy’s grandfather is dead and demands Kathy attend the funeral.  Even though Kathy hasn’t seen her grandfather in 15 years nor talked to her grandparents she ends up going.  I found it hard enough to believe that your roommate loves reading obituaries and felt it was appropriate to talk to you about it when it certainly felt like at the start of the game that Kathy is super abrasive and doesn’t get along much with Eileen.

Whatever, I got passed that.  Then you get to the funeral though and hear from your grandmother that after a strange incident in the woods your grandfather entered a catatonic state 15 years ago and medical professionals were baffled.  This leads Kathy to “take the case.”  No person would ever act this way, maybe some weird robot would, but no actual human ever.  For one, the incident happened 15 years ago, two no evidence really convinced Kathy this was anything other than a weird medical issue, three she didn’t feel the need to even talk to her grandparents before and now that her grandfather is dead shes going to investigate his medical problems? She literally storms off to the chief of police to interrogate him and then steal evidence to look into this issue? Maybe a sociopath would do this, but even that seems far fetched.

After Kathy learns her grandfather was investigating a woman’s suicide 16 years ago, Kathy seems to decide to investigate that as well? Shes a punk biker sophomore in college, shes a journalism major, but unlike Laura Bow she isn’t studious.  She apparently never attends class, and nothing leads me to suspect shes even a good journalism major, it’s not like she thinks, “oh what a scoop, I’m going to look into this.”  Her chief motivation seems to be guilt that her grandfather died and she didn’t know him so shes going to investigate this for some type of closure.  I just can’t accept that the way she attempts to find closure is to break a variety of laws to investigate what by all appearances is a medical issue. 

There are plenty of ways you could have written this story to work.  How about Kathy is a young detective on the police force in charge of a cold cases unit and is told to look into this girls suicide 16 years ago and through that discovers her grandfather who she was estranged from Kathy also was investigating it and then arrives to speak to her grandfather only to discover he just died?  Or how about Kathy gets a note from her grandmother telling her about how her grandfather was murdered days ago, not years, and Kathy rushes home and is sparked by this to investigate.  See that would make sense, what doesn’t make sense is finding out a medical issue 15 years ago put your grandfather in a catatonic state and you decide to “investigate” it when you have supposedly class the next day and you almost decide not to even bother going to the funeral.

Even then I could look passed allllllll of that if the rest of the story was good, but it’s not!  You can’t build a murder mystery without things like a cast of characters/suspects, dialogue/evidence, suspense, actual mystery.  The mystery is literally resolved in this game before it begins.  You learn people are disappearing a second later you discover the priest in the town is a serial killer murdering people.  I certainly suspected him, because he was literally the only character to really suspect other than either your roommate or your grandmother.  You don’t find much evidence pointing to him, but that doesn’t matter since he just straight up kidnaps and attempts to murder Eileen and you immediately know its him.  

Then there is the whole weird HP lovecraft old God thing, where a weird guy has been I guess taking souls to feed on?  It never really goes anywhere, you defeat his weird puzzle game at the end and burn down his weird old god ceremony seemingly defeating a God and the game ends.  If that sounds abrupt, it’s because it is, you know very little about him. You meet him throughout the game, but again the game is so short you don’t really get any feel for what he’s doing other than being evil [/spoiler]

Sigh, I was really hoping for a new Laura Bow style murder mystery, instead I got a mediocre horror story.  If you want to make a 10-12 hour Kathy Rain murder mystery with Eileen as her partner/girlfriend I would be up for that.  Otherwise…no…just no.

[h1][b]Kathy Rain			* 8/10[/b][/h1]

The first reason this game caught my attention was the nostalgic look. And it was worth it.

Kathy Rain is a good "old" point & click game with a low-res nostalgic look that could make you think this game came straight from the 90s.
And as a matter of fact the story takes place in the 90s: Kathy is studying journalism at college and lives at the dorm with her roommate Eileen and gets a phone call to be informed about her Grandfather's death. After the funeral, a chat with her Grandmother reveals some strange events that don't seem to add up, and that's where the real investigation begins.

As usual mouse is your friend, but for some odd reason the interface won't use your right click, as everything is set to work with the left click only. Besides that the interface is quite intuitive, so hovering with the cursor over usable items will make appear their names so you know you can use them, while items collected in your inventory can be examined, used or combined. Nothing new, but that's the point of reviving a classic, right? For some odd reason there are two different options for examining an item, and even though you don't get much more information then usual from them, I kind of liked the idea as classic P&C just have the same line for every item.

The soundtrack during the game is pleasant and appropirate, even though the title track and the travel track really are the only ones that really stand out.

Riddles are well built, nothing extremely complicated nor easy as a click (except for [spoiler]the scanner that can scan audio tapes, seriously, the last thing I could have thought of was examining a scanner to realize that...[/spoiler]), the best part of the game surely lies in the story that will take you around the town and let you talk with characters... Long and interesting talks. And the story (no spoilers) will really go deep to end up in an unexpected direction.

Definitely a really appreciated work, made with heart and mind, and with this I'm definitely keeping an eye on Clifftop Games. (no, I'm not paid by the publisher nor the developer. I just grew up with games like Monkey Island and Sam & Max)

[h1]+++PROs+++[/h1][list]
[*][b] STORY.[/b] What can I say, I have weakness for noir and detective stories, and I really had to force me to go to bed, otherwise I would have played the whole night (and slept instead of going to work)
[*][b] SOUNDTRACK.[/b] A pleasant soundtrack during the game and outstanding title track. Need anything else?
[*][b] RETRO' LOOK.[/b] Yes, growing up with Point & Click games from the 90s is something that can mark you. Seeing the images in the store page brought back memories of times where pixellous characters move in detailed backdrops, while during dialogues you can see detailed portraits of the speaking characters (as detailed as they can be in 320x200, of course)
[*][b] DIALOGUES AND CHARACTERS.[/b] Dialogues are the essence in this story. Much is being told during dialogues, part of stories, clues, references and useful informations. They're not useless or pointless even when it's just a general chat, as they still help you understand more the characters.
[/list]
[h1]---CONs---[/h1][list]
[*][b] DIALOGUES AUDIO.[/b] If I really really have to say something bad about something, well... Few dialogues have lower volume... That's it. Happy now?

I really enjoyed playing Kathy Rain.  If you like classic or retro style Point & Click Adventure games you’ll likely enjoy and appreciate this game.  I wouldn’t recommend it for those under 13 though simply because of the frequent cursing.  It does touch on some darker topics such as suicide and abortion but, doesn’t show much gore or anything regarding murders and deaths.

The story is pretty good, very interesting but could have been fleshed out a little more.  For example, they introduce a boy early on but the story around him is underdeveloped.  He seems like he should play a more important role but you seem him only briefly in a short cut scene and then as a minor plot device to move the ending forward.  The ending feels a little rushed and seems to be somewhat underdeveloped.

The premise of the story is that you find out your grandfather (who you’ve not seen for like 15 years) dies and you go his funeral and become interested in the mysterious cause of his long-term illness and eventual death.  As a journalism major you start investigating and it leads you to find out about several other deaths and illnesses and eventually leads you to some supernatural causes.  There are several intended plot twists but much of it was actually kind of predictable or at least partially predictable.  However, even if you can see what’s coming the story itself is interesting as it unfolds.

The characters in the story are for the most part well done.  I think there could have been a little more time fleshing out some of the characters and giving them more of a story arc.  Kathy Rain feels like she’s meant to have some major character development happening but it doesn’t feel like after everything happens that she’s actually worked through her past issues or shown much growth just accepted it enough to get through some tests and come out feeling largely unchanged.  I guess that this aspect of character development could have been much further developed and maybe it was intended to do so but the whole end feels a little rushed and maybe some of that was pared down to reach deadlines, budgets, or something along that line.  Some of the characters seem highly stereotyped but most I’d say are kind forgettable besides our main character.

The graphics of this game are done in a retro pixelated style common for 90’s games and retro styled games from the adventure games renaissance.  The pixelated graphics for the most part, are good.  Some odd sizing issues when the sprite has to move forward and backward on a scene but the left right mechanics are good.  The sprites are well drawn for their graphic size and the animations in general are smooth and have reasonably good walkpaths.  The backgrounds are well done and sufficiently display the environments and set the tone of the scenes.

The sound was good for this game.  Though the music is largely forgettable it did a good enough job of matching the tone and scene so that I never felt pulled out of the game by it.  It blended well to the setting; it just didn’t stand out as noticeable.  The voice recordings were well recorded, very professional sounding.  The voice acting was also really well done.  I was surprised by how well the voice actors did.  The conversations didn’t sound awkward or overly scripted and the actors were able to easily create natural sounding conversations.

There aren’t many puzzles in this game but, the few that are there are fairly logical and straightforward.  I did find the second part of the tomb puzzle near the end to be a little confusing and struggled with that for a while but most of the puzzles were moderately easy in my opinion.  Not so easy you don’t feel challenged at all but not so tough that you get overly frustrated with the game either.

The UI in this game is bare bones.  They tried to make the UI very simplistic.  This works in some ways but is frustrating (to me anyway) in others.  For example, in a typical P&C Adventure game you can select an item from your inventory the you see you’ve picked it up and you click it on something to try different reactions with various things in the inventory/environment.  Often you have multiple choices on your cursor to look, get, use, talk, etc…  which you then click on the item.  In this game however, you  click on the inventory item and then options appear around the item to look at it, think about it, use it, or combine it.  To use it in the environment around you, you must select combine and then click on the thing you want to use it with/on.  This feels like an extra step to me and I found that method of interacting to be a little annoying but, I think it’s just a personal preference.  It works fine but, it’s not my preference for interacting with the game.  The other thing I don’t really like is there is no access to the menu for saving, loading, changing options, etc… right in the screen or with a mouse-over spot somewhere on the screen.  You can access that menu by pressing esc but, I prefer to have access to it a little more obvious.  There is not worry about pixel hunting with this game as it shows hotspots by pressing the spacebar so if you hate pixel hunting then you’ll love this feature.

There are 20 achievements in this game.  5 of those unlock through story completion but the rest require special actions, repeated actions, or in some cases … alack of action.  All of the achievements are obtainable in 1 playthrough but unless you are using a guide I’m guessing many people would be missing a good half of the remaining 15 achievements.  Many are not something you would come across naturally.  Do pay attention to what Kathy says about things when she looks at or thinks about them.  Sometime she gives clues that indicate something you could do for an achievement.

I did my first playthrough in about 4.5 hours and then played half way through for a missing achievement in about 1.5 hours.  I’d say this game probably is a 4-6 hr game depending on your familiarity with P&C games and how long certain puzzles take you.  At. 4.5 hours it’s about $3.33/hr of gameplay.  I don’t think it has a huge amount of replay value though.  At that price point it is a little too pricey.  If however you can get it on sale, it’s well worth it.

The truly disappointing thing about Kathy Rain is that it's ultimately HALF of a really good game. It starts out as an atmospheric small-town mystery. and Kathy herself is obviously trying a bit too hard to be a "tough girl" protagonist, but you get the continuous sense that she's intentionally overdoing it in order to hide the emotional problems she very clearly has, and for the most part I'm on board with that. The relationship with her roommate feels genuine underneath all the snark. The atmosphere is palpable, there were several moments that made me smile, and some of the puzzles are remarkable - in that they're challenging, clever and fitting for what you're trying to do without falling into the loop-de-loop bizarro logic normally employed by point and click adventure games.

Those are the good bits. 

The game goes off the rails - and it goes off the rails HARD - when it tries to take a leaf out of the playbook of the much better established Blackwell series and decides to take a turn for the supernatural. Nothing in the plot adds up satisfyingly, everything piles incomprehensibly on top of each other, and you get the growing sense that the supernatural twist was added simply because the developer thought "This worked for Blackwell, right?!" and an "ordinary" murder mystery wouldn't sell well enough. Which is sad.

And for a final, damning nail in the coffin, the game then tries to do the whole "disturbing psychological HORRORRRRR/protagonist's CREEPY confrontation with herself" thing as established by Silent Hill and (particularly) American McGee's Alice, and it just doesn't *work* because the buildup of those games isn't there. It's about as jarring a tonal shift as you can imagine - the low point being the protagonist's father imagined as a zombie-like bogeyman chasing her - and just feels like a desperate attempt to grab attention because "look how distuuuuuurrrrbiiiiiiing."

The less I say about the game's handling of the topic of abortion, the better.

Good, solid detective game.  Worth your time.

Story and characterization are excellent.  The heroine is likeable enough for player-identification, but has enough of a personality to be memorable on her own, a balance many games fail to strike.  Voice actors range from decent to very good.  The comic relief homeless guy is annoying and overdrawn, but he is the exception that proves the rule of a sympathetic and believable cast.

One nice feature is the game's tendency to clean up after itself.  Once an inventory item or conversation topic has been exhausted, it often disappears.  Some clutter persists to the end game, but it could have been much worse.

Game is about 8 hours, which ran a little long for my taste.  Also, there is no in-game journal keeping track of characters and events.  Play this game all at once, say in 2-3 sessions over a week at the most; otherwise you will risk forgetting important information and the game has no mechanisms to remind you.  I played the game over just 2 weeks and by the end I had to look up the names of people I'd met because there is no record of them.

That's the only downside, though.  Overall this is a solid example of how an adventure and/or detective game should play.  Grab it.

[i]Kathy Rain[/i] is a very well thought-out supernatural mystery set in a small town in the Pacific Northwest.  It starts out, of course, like an ordinary mystery, with the heroine following threads that are surprisingly logical and believable in the course of investigating her grandfather's odd death -- but then things start to get spectral and culty in the classiest of ways.  The tone of the adventure is predominately serious, but Kathy can't help but engage in a few cheeky high jinks of the sort that are hardwired into every point-and-click protagonist's DNA.  Personally, if I don't get to do a little Threepwoodish trollery in an adventure, something just feels [i]off[/i].

If you are skittish about episodic games, know that this is not one, whatever the title suggests.  It's an awesome, self-contained adventure that [i]might[/i] get a well-deserved sequel, more than worth the time of any genre fan.

What starts off as a intriguing mystery game soon turns a lot creepier and darker than you expect. There's also a huge amount of the game that can be interpreted in many ways, which I think really keeps the mystery going. Ultimately, it is more than about what happened to her grandfather, and a lot about Kathy struggling to put the past behind her.

The game itself, while a little shorter than some similar games (I initially found it remeniscent of games like The Longest Journey, and there's quite a similarity between the two protagonists), has a mostly strong story. There are a couple of things that could have been elaborated on, and some that seemed to go on for too long, but that's the same with any game like this. The way you do things is not completely rigid, but you don't get the same aspect of control over everything - for example, while you occasionally get the options for different responses to people, most of the time it seems to have no future effect.

The puzzles in the game are quite well thought-out, though at times they are not obvious, and you might find yourself reaching for a walkthrough once or twice. There's nothing that doesn't make sense once you've done it, but a few (such as getting the clinic receptionist away from her desk) aren't what most would think of doing.

There also seems to be a running theme of mental illness throughout the game, and it's great to see it dealt with outside of the usual serial killer/unintelligible rambler tropes. Kathy is clearly troubled by the difficulties of those around her, despite her attitude, and it's subtly played throughout the game as she turns from a feisty no-s**ts-given biker chick, to a vulnerable woman whose past is possibly leading her to the same fate as her mother.

Overall, I would absolutely recommend this game. It brings up more emotions than you'd initially expect, and while quite short, the story is fantastic and it's well worth the money.

[h1]Story and Protagonist[/h1]
   The Story follows Kathy Rain, a journalism student, who gets confronted with her childhood and family struggles after attending her grandfather's funeral whom she hasn't seen for years.

In the beginning I was a tad bit concerned about Kathy as a protagonist because even tho I liked her from the start she also felt intentionally edgy and "not like other girls". This concern was unneccessary tho and she as well as her friendship with Eileen grew on me. Especially near the end you can truly understand why Kathy became such a sarcastic and sometimes harsh person. (Not that she isn't funny or compassionate.)

Overall the plot was weird but I liked it.
I can totally see why some may be disappointed by the ending. It wasn't outright illogical or anything but too open for my taste. A lot of things were left without proper explanation and I wanted to know more.
At least there was somewhat of emotional closure for Kathy tho.

[h1]Praise[/h1]
   The thing that really stuck out to me - besides the pretty pixel graphics and the good voice acting - was the functionality of the interface and dialogue. It really makes the game so much more enjoyable that Kathy has her notebook where she writes down dialogue options and she remembers for herself what she already asked so most of the time you won't need to ask a greyed out option twice. She also updates it when getting new information not only crossing out stuff but also tweaking it a bit. This gives you a satisfying feeling of progression in your work as a detective.

[h1]Difficulty and Achievements[/h1]
   Difficulty is okay. I got stuck and had to look up a few things but I wasn't tryharding most of the time. So if you have some experience with Point & Click Adventures (I don't really), a bit of patience and are focused on the game I doubt you'll have any troubles. Otherwise you can always either try everything until something works (Calling E. for advice is also very helpful in the beginning) or look up your next step in some neat guide on steam.

Achievements are also doable. Fun and not too outlandish. I got the missing ones after my first playthrough with a guide but I feel like you could get them just by paying attention.
Also be sure to save a few different times in your playthrough so that you don't have to do another full one to get to 100%. Exploring every possibility helps and often doing the rude thing gives you an achievement.

The only real irritation was the main character. She feels a little too perfect: sarcastic, witty, endlessly resourceful, rides a Harley—you get the picture. But even so, she has enough depth and surprises to avoid feeling flat.

I sincerely hope the game gets a sequel someday.

The game goes out of its way to investigate trauma later on in a particularly uninspired way. The protagonist seems insincere at every point of the experience, though that could be my extreme dislike of them speaking.

Suggested improvements:
Apparently there is a remake/extended edition on the horizon for this game. Hopefully they develop everything a little more without killing pace. I would be interested in knowing more about literally everyone one of the side characters. 
There is ample room here for some side plots intertwined with the main story, and even some optional bits that aren’t. (Dave vs Clyde, More about the base and gramp’s history, etc.)

I think closing off areas the player doesn’t need to go to was a nice idea, but for me it detracted from red herrings I’d created for myself. I’d reopen those places and allow the player to roam, but I acknowledge that runs the risk of damaging the snappy pacing of the game. 

Overall recommendation:
Overall I recommend this game. It isn’t an old school adventure, but it’s a damn good tribute. I suspect most people will actually enjoy it more than me because they won’t hate the protagonist. So I give it a thumbs up, even if I don’t particularly want to.

This game's 90s heritage goes much deeper than a 4:3 window and 16-bit sprites. That said, the above is what makes the difference between a reccommendation and an enthusiastic reccommendation. Whatever you go into Kathy Rain looking for you're probably going to find it. This one is really hard. I liked a lot about it. Kathy herself is fun to play up to a point. Her roommate is also a solid character, and the interplay between the two of them could have been a lot better than it was. There are strong hints that this is the first game in a series, and that Kathy and Eileen will be a team. I think that could be really cool.

Ultimately, though, there just wasn't all that much to recommend the game. The puzzle design isn't stellar, at all, and there are a lot of places where you can easily get stuck while the game waits for you to do some specific thing to trigger the end of the day or some other event that doesn't seem directly related. There's a lot of gating to the puzzles that feels arbitrary and which you can easily get hung up on. There are a lot of times when, as a player, I wanted to pursue lead X, but the game doesn't want you to look at that until tomorrow, so you have to do unrelated tasks Y, Z, A, and B in order to get access to that. 

Perhaps most disappointing for the experience, though, is that there's very little latitude to role-play Kathy. On several occasions you have to do things that I just plain didn't want to do, and which felt optional -- a different approach to a puzzle, say. Upon looking up a walkthrough it always turned out that, no, you have to do that or the game won't move forward.

The final sequence has a satisfying set of not-too-hard but reasonable and logical puzzles that wind it up on a positive note, gameplay wise, but it's all marred by some weird moral messages right at the end. Also, there are elements to the story that really don't seem to hang together well, or which seemed tacked on at the last moment.

The other issue is, in broad terms, some of the needlessly retro elements. I'd be going about my business trying to solve a murder when suddenly I need to trick a college student out of an admin password or make a wacky beverage for a biker gang. STOP ACTING LIKE THIS TO EVERYONE YOU MEET." It doesn't help that the main character is asocial, manipulative and introduced so poorly that any sympathy flies out the window.

I get the idea is for Kathy to feel really cool when she snarks and curses her way out of everything, but to me it only sounds like a Mary Sue. A self-absorbed perfect character who can do nothing wrong and will always get away scot-free. She doesn't even get a stern look from a man she tazered as a distraction - this isn't Day of the Tentacle, this is supposed to be taken seriously.

It gets even better when the game has an abortion subplot. Heavy subject in a seriously toned video games? Sure, I can roll with that - so how does it go? [b]Spoilers ahead if you care.[/b]

1. You introduce the abortion in a dream about the past of the main character.

I was initially dismissive of *Kathy Rain*. After playing the demo, I thought it felt too much like a weaker imitation of *Gabriel Knight* and the *Blackwell* series. Giving it a second chance changed my mind.

The influence is certainly there, but *Kathy Rain* has enough personality of its own. It belongs to that familiar but effective subgenre of supernatural detective adventures: an apparently ordinary mystery gradually opens into something darker and stranger.

Kathy herself initially looks like a stock rebellious college student - leather jacket, cigarettes, motorcycle, dyed hair - but the family history behind that persona gives her considerably more depth. The story begins when she returns home for her grandfather's funeral after years of estrangement, and her reunion with her grandmother sets off an investigation into long-buried events.

The grounded mystery and character work are stronger than the overtly supernatural side of the story. In fact, one of my strongest memories of the game is that the final, more nightmarish stretch felt like its weakest part. Some of the story elements never quite came together into a fully satisfying ending.

That said, the journey there works extremely well.

The pixel art is beautiful, the voice acting is excellent, and the puzzles are generally challenging without becoming frustrating. I only needed help a couple of times, and most solutions felt fair.

It took me about five hours to finish, which felt like the right length.

*Kathy Rain* is not quite on the level of the games that inspired it, but it is a very good adventure in the same tradition, with a strong protagonist, an engaging mystery, and a world I would happily return to. In fact, rereading my old review made me want to drop everything and play it again.

Kathy Rain is a narrative-focused adventure that blends classic point-and-click design with a deeply personal mystery, resulting in an experience that feels both nostalgic and emotionally grounded. Set in the mid-1990s, the game follows Kathy Rain, a sharp-tongued journalism student who returns to her hometown after the death of her grandfather. What begins as a seemingly straightforward investigation into his passing slowly unfolds into a layered story about family trauma, small-town secrets, and the lasting scars left by unresolved events. From the opening moments, the game establishes a strong sense of place and character, drawing players into a world that feels lived-in and quietly troubled.

Kathy herself is one of the game’s greatest strengths. She is portrayed as intelligent, stubborn, and emotionally guarded, shaped by a difficult upbringing and strained family relationships. Her dialogue is often sarcastic and blunt, but beneath that exterior lies a character driven by curiosity and unresolved grief. This makes her investigation feel personal rather than procedural, as each discovery connects not just to the mystery at hand but also to her own identity and past. The writing does an excellent job of letting her personality shine through natural conversations rather than heavy exposition, making her feel like a fully realized protagonist rather than a genre archetype.

The gameplay adheres closely to traditional point-and-click mechanics, emphasizing exploration, dialogue, and inventory-based puzzles. Players move between locations, talk to locals, gather clues, and gradually piece together information through careful observation. The puzzles are generally logical and grounded in the narrative, avoiding excessive obscurity and encouraging players to think contextually about the world and its characters. While there are moments of increased difficulty, these tend to arise from narrative complexity rather than arbitrary design, keeping frustration to a minimum and maintaining immersion.

Narratively, Kathy Rain excels at building tension through gradual revelation. As Kathy digs deeper into her grandfather’s history, the story widens to encompass other residents of Conwell Springs, each with their own memories and secrets. The pacing allows the mystery to breathe, layering personal drama, investigative intrigue, and unsettling implications without rushing to conclusions. The game takes a bold turn into darker and more surreal territory as it progresses, a choice that may surprise some players but ultimately reinforces the story’s themes of obsession, repression, and the cost of uncovering hidden truths.

Visually, the game embraces a detailed pixel art style that pays homage to classic adventure games while still feeling contemporary. The environments are richly atmospheric, using lighting, color, and composition to convey mood rather than realism. Conwell Springs feels isolated and slightly decayed, reinforcing the sense that the town is holding onto secrets it would rather forget. The soundtrack complements this perfectly, combining moody ambient tracks with melodic themes that underscore both quiet reflection and moments of tension.

The Director’s Cut version further enhances the experience by refining visuals, expanding locations, and adding full voice acting. These additions strengthen character interactions and make emotional beats land more effectively, without altering the core structure that made the original release compelling. The voice performances, in particular, add nuance to conversations and help distinguish the personalities of the supporting cast, making the town feel more alive and believable.

Overall, Kathy Rain is a thoughtfully crafted adventure that stands out through its strong protagonist, grounded mystery, and confident storytelling. It respects the traditions of classic point-and-click games while updating them with modern pacing and emotional depth. Though its length is relatively modest, the experience feels complete and purposeful, leaving a lasting impression through its characters and themes rather than sheer scale. For players who appreciate narrative-driven games with a focus on character and atmosphere, Kathy Rain remains a standout example of how powerful a well-told mystery can be.

First things first...For those that say this is similar to Gabriel Knight......get your fu**ing head examined. There is absolutely no comparison. 

I love adventure games. My father got me hooked on them when I was little....I remember as a kid I would help him (or try to) solve the old sierra games. I feel like a veteran in this genre...with that being said..........

 Kathy Rain does not live up to my personal standards of what I believe an adventure game should be. Its not terrible......but its not good either. Those that have different standards than me will obviously disagree.

One of the main problems is the story and lets be honest, thats what makes or breaks an adventure game. The story feels forced.....like the writers raped the story into this game. As the story progressed I found myself becoming more disappointed than excited. It is supposed to be set in the 90's and other than the story telling me it was 1995. I didn't feel any connection to that decade whatsoever. The protagonist, Kathy Rain, is a cardboard cut out of the classic 90's rebellious edgy teen with a bleeding heart. Kathy didn't feel like a real character but more of a stereotype of what some idiot writer had in mind for the story. 

The story starts off with Kathy coming into her dorm drunk and wanting to sleep it off.  Then Emily, her little stereotypical Christian roommate, tells her she has been doing research on Kathy's hometown because..the writers needed the story to advance and tells her she found out that a man, Joseph Rain had died recently. This is her grandfather and despite being gone for 15 years she decides to attend the funeral and start doing investigations......because the writers needed the story to advance. The games handles story progression this way.... ALL......THE..... FUCK**G..... TIME.....

The puzzles are even worse than the story.....If you are looking for challenging puzzles....Try grabbing a brick and smashing it to your head about 5 times before you play this game. The swelling of your brain might make them more difficult to solve. 

All of the characters in this game are cardboard cutouts of stereotypes. This is why you don't get shitty writers to make your game. 

I won't reveal any spoilers but....the ending didnt answer any questions......fortunatly the story sucked so badly that I didnt care. 

Note: I fell asleep playing this game...so the hours spent on this game can be misleading. The game can be completed in 6-7 hours. (no walkthroughs)

Neat little Point and Click Adventure. Old School Graphics and a very nice soundtrack. Puzzles are more on the easier side and there are very few of them.
The great story really is the core of the game. If you ever watched any David Lynch movie, or Twin Peaks, then you will find a lot of similarities. It starts a bit slow, but accelerate real quickly. It may be even a bit too packed at the end, but still great. It will leave you with an urge for more episodes to come.

While full price may be a bit too much for about 8 hours of gameplay, it's totally worth it on sale, especially if you like the genre.
The game is completely different from what I expected. Very nicely implemented though. Puzzles were not frustrating, decent narration, great graphics. Definitely worth the money.

This is a superb game on many levels. The sense of mystery hooks you in very quickly and the story does a great job of not being overly predictable or cliched with a very strong finish. The characters are fun and interesting and feel real. Unlike so many other point-and-click games, the puzzles aren't overly hard and some of them (can't help but think of the hacking voice synthesis thing) are wonderfully creative. The art style is strong, with a very nostalgic 90's era feel. The sound and music are good. The dialogue is a lot of fun and makes the characters feel relatable. If you're looking for a point-and-click adventure game with a great storyline this is it! Thanks to everyone involved for creating something so cool. :)

Meh. If you are looking for an old-style point-and-click adventure game, this isn't it. 
The pixel art is nice and brings back to memory the LucasArts titles, but nostalgia only takes you so far. There is a lot of talking, a lot, and not enough puzzles. The ending is underwhelming and comes out of left field.
So, if you are looking for an adventure game with brain teasers: no.
If you are looking for a sentimental, coming of age story, with supernatural vibes: yes, you will enjoy the story and the characters. 
The game would be much more enjoyable if they hadn't titles it "A detective is born". It's misleading and doesn't make any favours.

This game surprised me in a number of ways.  First off, I was not convined the "badass motorcycle riding leather jacket wearing 90's chick" could be pulled of without feeling extremely cringey.  I'm happy to report that not only did they make her feel more grounded and realistic than I thought, she was a delight of a main character with a well fleshed out backstory.  Her character is definitely what held this game together.

I was also not expecting the game to first dabble in and then fully dive in to the [spoiler]supernatural[/spoiler] the way it did.  To be honest, I preferred the earlier parts of the game that worked more as a burgeoning detective/investigative journalists origin story than what came later, but I will admit there was some pretty cool moments and imagery later in the game.

For a first time release, this was really an excellent showing and I'm interested to see what else this dev can make.

It was so fun! I'm a long-time Nancy Drew game fan and I've also enjoyed the Lucas Arts games and this was a great combination of the two. It was reminiscent of Twin Peaks and Stranger Things. I think it was intuitive, rewarding, and well-written. Now I'm going to try the other games in the series, I really recommend this game to anyone wanting a classic mystery game.

I was wanting to play a point and click adventure and got this game on sale. I would say I enjoyed it, the story was compelling enough for me to want to finish it, plus the game isn't particularly long (it took about 5 hours to complete). The puzzles required some thought but weren't too challenging which is nice! 

I wasn't sure how to feel about Kathy as a protagonist. While I liked that she was strong-willed, I thought she was borderline mean in some parts but this was supposed to be seen as.. cool? Also the "I'm not like most girls" line... jesus. Yeah that was goofy. It's possible to write a strong female protagonist without resorting to that 'edginess'. It was nice to see her open up more emotionally later in the game, however. 

The depictions of mental illness and neurodivergency were a little stale too. I understand the game is set in the 90's, but I think some things could have been done better (e.g. the infantalisation of Nathan). 

The ending felt a little rushed, but I was fine to shrug it off since the game was short. Overall I did enjoy it! If another Kathy Rain game came out, I'd play it, but in the hopes that they write Kathy a little better.
